name: Stanford HAI AI Index: landing page for the annual AI Index report series
title: Stanford HAI AI Index: landing page for the annual AI Index report series
answer: This is Stanford HAI's AI Index landing page, describing an independent annual program that tracks, collates, distills and visualizes data on artificial intelligence for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the public. Its most useful claim for nonprofits is that this year's Index finds a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared institutions are to manage it, with governance, evaluation and understanding frameworks falling behind while technical capabilities, investment and adoption advance. It also notes declining data transparency, making independent measurement more critical.

sections.body: Stanford HAI publishes this AI Index landing page. It describes the AI Index as an independent initiative at Stanford HAI, led by an interdisciplinary AI Index Steering Committee with experts from academia and industry. The page presents the program's mission, highlights from this year's Index, recognition and citations, related research, a collaboration, and support information. It says the 2026 Stanford AI Index Report was released this month and that this year's edition surpasses previous ones in size, scale and scope. The page was harvested on 29 September 2026.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The AI Index mission is to provide unbiased, rigorously vetted and globally sourced data for policymakers, researchers, journalists, executives and the general public. It tracks, collates, distills and visualizes data relating to artificial intelligence. This year's Index reveals a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared we are to manage it. AI continues its rapid integration into the global economy, with technical capabilities improving, investment accelerating and adoption spreading, but the frameworks needed to govern, evaluate and understand the technology are falling behind. In a field where data transparency is declining, the page says independent, rigorous measurement has never been more critical, and it calls the report the most comprehensive analysis of AI's trajectory available. Stanford HAI says AI is poised to be the most transformative technology of the 21st century, but its benefits will not be evenly distributed unless development is guided thoughtfully. The AI Index is described as recognized globally as one of the most credible and authoritative sources for data and insights on AI. Previous editions have been cited in The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, have amassed hundreds of academic citations, and been referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. The page also says the program writes about AI progress and impact through a cross-sector lens, from research and development to technical performance, the economy, education and policy.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source states that previous editions have amassed hundreds of academic citations and were cited in The New York Times, Bloomberg and The Guardian, and referenced by high-level policymakers in the United States, the United Kingdom and the European Union. It says a related paper identifies six summary challenges in measuring AI progress and impact and summarizes over 40 presentations from a fall 2019 Stanford workshop. It names the 2026 AI Index Report and says it was released this month. It also names Dr. Elif Kiesow Cortez and the AI & LegTech Lab of The Hague University of Applied Sciences for a judicial decision database project, and HAI Executive Director Russell Wald and AI Index Lead Sha Sajadieh in discussions about U.S. and China AI competition, world models, and American and Chinese public sentiment. A quoted passage says the 2026 report notes a sharp increase in AI adoption in medicine, including clinical documentation, medical imaging and diagnostic reasoning.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: The source does not discuss nonprofits directly. A reader following AI in nonprofits would use it as a macro reference because it claims to offer globally sourced, cross-sector data on AI's technical progress, economic influence and societal impact, and because it says policymakers, researchers, journalists and executives are its intended audiences. Its claim that governance, evaluation and understanding frameworks are falling behind while adoption spreads is relevant to nonprofit readers assessing readiness and oversight. Its stated cross-sector lens includes education and policy, which can inform nonprofit work in those areas, but the page itself gives no nonprofit-specific findings or implementation guidance.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Nonprofits

sections.body: This is a landing page, not the full report. It gives highlights and claims, not the underlying data, methodology or sector-level findings. It does not mention nonprofits or give nonprofit-specific adoption, funding or governance figures. The page promotes the Index, describing it as the most comprehensive analysis and as globally recognized, and it asks for philanthropic support. It is dated by the harvested page and by the statement that the 2026 report was released this month. The quoted medical adoption passage is cut off, so it cannot be assessed fully. The page also links to related talks and a 2019 measurement paper, but those are separate items.
